title: Star’s Record Eruption Reveals How Key Elements Travel Across Space【Phys.org】
body:
Astronomers have captured the most detailed view yet of a massive stellar eruption, revealing how elements forged in a star’s core can be hurled into interstellar space. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, an international team led by Wouter Vlemmings and Miora Andriantsaralaza of Chalmers University of Technology imaged the explosive outflow from the red supergiant VY Canis Majoris, a nearby star whose violent eruptions are thought to seed the galaxy with the building blocks of planets and life. The observations, which resolve the ejected material at unprecedented spatial resolution, show that heavy elements such as silicon, sulfur and iron are dispersed in clumps that survive the harsh conditions of the stellar wind, offering fresh insight into the chemical enrichment of the Milky Way.

The breakthrough came from a series of high‑frequency ALMA observations that traced the distribution of molecular gas and dust in the star’s circumstellar envelope. By targeting specific emission lines of silicon monoxide (SiO), sulfur monoxide (SO) and other metal‑bearing molecules, the researchers were able to map the three‑dimensional structure of the eruption. The data reveal a tangled web of filaments and knots extending several hundred astronomical units from the star, each knot containing a distinct chemical fingerprint. This level of detail surpasses previous studies that could only infer the presence of heavy elements from bulk spectra, and it confirms that the star’s violent mass‑loss episodes are far more heterogeneous than the smooth, spherical winds long assumed in stellar models.

VY Canis Majoris, located roughly 4,000 light‑years from Earth, is one of the most massive and luminous red supergiants known, teetering on the brink of a supernova. Its erratic behavior has made it a natural laboratory for studying the late stages of stellar evolution, when nuclear fusion in the core creates elements heavier than helium. As the star exhausts its fuel, convective currents dredge these newly forged atoms to the surface, where they are expelled by powerful stellar winds. The new ALMA images demonstrate that this expulsion is not a gentle, uniform process; instead, it occurs in violent, localized eruptions that fling clumps of enriched material far into the surrounding interstellar medium.

The findings have broad implications for our understanding of galactic chemistry. Heavy elements released by dying stars eventually become part of the gas clouds that form new generations of stars and planets. By quantifying how these elements are packaged and distributed, astronomers can refine models of star formation and the lifecycle of matter in the galaxy. Moreover, the detection of dense, metal‑rich knots suggests that some of the ejected material may survive long enough to seed nearby molecular clouds, potentially influencing the composition of future planetary systems.

The study also showcases ALMA’s capability to probe the fine‑scale physics of stellar outflows. The array’s combination of high sensitivity and angular resolution allows researchers to dissect the anatomy of stellar eruptions in a way that was previously impossible. Future observations of other red supergiants and massive stars will test whether the clumpy, chemically diverse outflows seen in VY Canis Majoris are common or exceptional. If such eruptions prove to be a universal feature of late‑stage massive stars, they could account for a significant fraction of the heavy elements observed throughout the Milky Way.

Looking ahead, the team plans to monitor VY Canis Majoris over the coming years to track the evolution of its ejecta and to search for signs of an impending supernova. Continued ALMA campaigns, complemented by data from upcoming infrared and optical facilities, will enable a more complete picture of how dying stars recycle their material back into the cosmos. As astronomers piece together these processes, each new observation brings us closer to understanding the cosmic origins of the elements that make up everything from distant nebulae to the very atoms in our bodies.
